source.name: Doo-wop
source.lineage: Late-1940s through early-1960s African-American (originally) and Italian-American (East Coast urban) vocal-harmony group teen-pop R&B tradition built on the I-vi-IV-V chord cycle and non-lexical vocal syllables (shooby-doo-wop) — the Orioles, the Ravens, the Five Satins, the Penguins (Earth Angel, 1954), the Platters, Frankie Lymon and the Teenagers (Why Do Fools Fall in Love, 1956)

extras.description: Doo-wop (codified 1953-1963 in African-American urban centers, with the New York / New Jersey / Philadelphia / Cincinnati / Chicago / Los Angeles vocal-group scenes producing the recordings, and the form fading from popular foreground after the British Invasion of 1964 and the rise of Motown soul superseded the simpler vocal-group template), the African-American vocal-harmony group tradition that bridges the late-1940s jubilee-and-gospel-quartet lineage with the early-1960s soul vocal-group lineage. Defined by lead-vocal-and-backing-quartet-or-quintet ensemble configuration with the lead singer carrying melody-and-narrative-lyric while three or four backing voices supply harmony underpinning, the syllabic-nonsense-vocable backing-line device (the "doo-wop", "shoo-be-doo", "shoo-doo-de-doo" patterning that names the genre) functioning as harmonic-and-rhythmic foundation in place of and in addition to instrumental rhythm-section, light rhythm-section accompaniment (electric guitar, electric bass replacing upright bass through the era, drum kit with brush-or-stick subdued backbeat, occasional saxophone solo break, occasional piano, never overly busy — the vocals carry the song), I-vi-IV-V ("doo-wop progression") and similar simple cyclic chord changes that became the foundational template for early rock-and-roll and pop ballad writing, and lyric content centered on adolescent romantic experience (the "teenager"-as-cultural-category emerging exactly contemporaneous with the genre, both as marketing target and as the subjects the songs depicted). Cultural origin: jubilee-quartet sacred-vocal lineage rerouted toward secular romantic material via the late-1940s rhythm-and-blues vocal-group transition (the Mills Brothers, the Ink Spots), with mid-1950s urban-storefront and street-corner amateur quartets supplying the bulk of the era's recording roster (one-hit-wonder economics characteristic of the genre — most groups recorded only one or two records before dissolving). Distinguished from contemporaneous classic R&B by vocal-group-foreground over instrumental-band-foreground and by harmonic-vocable backing over horn-section backing; distinguished from preceding jubilee quartet by secular-romantic over sacred-spiritual subject matter; distinguished from following Motown soul by simpler cyclic chord vocabulary and by absence of orchestral-pop production scale. Lineage forward feeds the 1960s soul vocal-group tradition (the Drifters bridge group), the 1960s girl-group tradition (the Brill Building songwriters who scored doo-wop hits also wrote for the Crystals and Ronettes), and through them the broader pop-vocal-harmony lineage extending to street-corner-revival a-cappella movements of the 1970s onward.

extras.description: Goth crystallized in Britain between 1979 and 1985 as post-punk's darkest, most theatrical branch, built on reverb-saturated chorused guitar, prominent melodic bass, and either tom-led tribal drumming or a rigidly programmed drum machine. It is distinguished from generic post-punk by its committed aesthetic of decay and ritual, and from later industrial and darkwave by remaining guitar-centered rather than synthesizer-driven.
